title: Fluid windowing coordinator — experiments and sketch
content:
Overview:

This is a working sketch for a "fluid windowing coordinator" as an alternative/augmentation to the current token-level vs request-level continuous batching debate. The goal: reduce unnecessary kernel churn and KV-cache thrashing while preserving per-request latency SLOs and improving long-request throughput fairness. This doc collects rationale, allocator rules, kernel affinity heuristics, and an experiment matrix to validate tradeoffs.

Key ideas (TL;DR):
- Use soft, dynamic windows that adapt size based on live request mix and kernel compatibility instead of fixed token slices.
- Maintain lightweight per-window metadata: kernel_signature, model_variant, kv_affinity_tag, token_budget_remaining, priority_epoch.
- Prefer coalescing tokens into windows that share kernel_signature and similar sequence-length percentiles to reduce kernel rebinds and optimize memory locality.
- Implement micro-preemption: windows can donate unused token-budget to higher-priority short requests when idle, with accounting to preserve long-request fairness (credit rebalance).

Why this direction?
- Token-level batching is great for maximizing throughput, but: kernel switches and KV-cache hotset misses can negate benefits in heterogenous workloads.
- Request-level fairness (allocating whole requests preferentially) preserves per-request latency but often underutilizes GPU cores for short (few-token) requests.
- Fluid windows aim to get the best of both: keep kernel/coherence advantages of grouped tokens while allowing on-the-fly redistribution across concurrent requests.

Coordinator components (sketch):
1) Admission controller (fast path)
   - Accepts incoming request, computes quick headers: model, quantization, prompt_length_estimate, user_priority_tag, kv_hint (customer-provided or hashed conversation id).
   - If immediate short-circuit path (very small request and free capacity) send to short-window fast lane.
2) Window selector
   - Maintains active windows per GPU worker. For each window stores kernel_signature, kv_affinity_tag, target_token_capacity, current_fill, last_activity_ts.
   - Scoring function for candidate windows: score = w1*kernel_match + w2*kv_affinity + w3*remaining_capacity_compatibility - w4*inactivity_penalty + w5*priority_boost. Values are tunable.
3) Window allocator / resizer
   - If no candidate window meets score threshold, allocate new window sized by current short/long mix and target_core_utilization. Windows start small, can grow up to a configured cap.
   - Growth policy: proportional to recent short-request fraction; shrink on idle timescale.
4) Micro-preemption & credit accounting
   - Windows accumulate "latency credits" proportional to how much earlier they yielded tokens to other requests. Credits can be redeemed later to borrow tokens or get scheduling priority. This prevents long-request starvation while allowing opportunistic repayment.
5) Kernel affinity hints & compaction
   - When two windows on same worker have identical kernel_signature and compatible quantization, allow compaction: merge windows (if total token count fits cap) to avoid kernel switch and KV shuffles. Compaction happens in background at epoch boundaries.
6) KV-cache pinning heuristic
   - Track per-window KV-hit-rate estimate using sampling. For windows with high KV affinity and long tails, prefer to keep them contiguous (avoid splitting across kernel epochs).

Fairness definitions and goals:
- Short-tail fairness: 95th and 99th percentile latency for requests <= 32 tokens should be close to baseline (<+10% overhead).
- Long-request liveness: Median throughput for requests >= 512 tokens should not regress more than X% (configurable) over request-level allocator baseline.
- Kernel-stability metric: kernel_switches_per_minute (lower is better).
- KV-hit-rate: fraction of KV cache accesses that hit (higher is better).
- Economic fairness: per-customer token-cost variance should not allow a small noisy tenant to push cost externalities onto others beyond configured quotas.

Policy knobs (configurable):
- kernel_match_weight, kv_affinity_weight, priority_boost_scale
- initial_window_size_tokens, max_window_size_tokens, window_growth_rate, shrink_idle_ms
- credit_earn_rate_per_token_yielded, credit_spend_limit_per_request
- compaction_interval_ms, compaction_threshold_tokens

Operational considerations:
- Complexity: coordinator maintains more live state per worker; must be memory/lightweight and robust under churn. We should guard expensive scoring/evaluation with fast-path heuristics and use sampling for heavy metrics.
- Backpressure: if windows saturate, provide early fallback to request-level strict scheduling (configurable emergency mode).
- Observability: expose per-window metrics (fill, kernel_sig, kv_hit_est, credits) to console; add trace hooks for kernel switch events.
- Safety: default to conservative settings; disable compaction when KV-cache is cold (startup).

Experiment plan:
1) Microbench harness scenarios (locally + staging):
   A: Short-heavy: 90% requests <= 16 tokens, 10% long (>=512 tokens).
   B: Balanced: 60% short(<=32), 30% mid(64–256), 10% long(>=512).
   C: Noisy-tenant: single tenant sends bursty long-requests while others short.
   D: Kernel-heterogeneous: two models with different kernel signatures receive interleaved requests.

Metrics to collect:
- p50/p95/p99 per-size bucket (short/mid/long)
- tokens/sec GPU utilization, kernel_switches/min, kv_hit_rate, average window_compaction_events, credits_earned/spent distribution per-request
- tail fairness delta vs existing continuous-batcher baseline

A/B test plan (staging -> canary -> prod):
- Stage 1 (staging): run harness A–D, tune weights to hit short-tail latency SLOs without >10% throughput regression on long requests.
- Stage 2 (canary): route 5% of traffic on dedicated canary fleet; compare telemetry and error budgets for 48h.
- Stage 3 (ramp): 25% then 50% if stable. Rollback triggers: p99_short > baseline+15% or kernel_switches increase >2x with backend QoS regressions.

Open questions / risks:
- How to choose kernel_signature granularity? (function-level vs compiled-kernel-id). Finer granularity increases matchability but risks misclassification when micro-kernels change.
- Credit accounting manipulation: tenants may game priority by generating fake short-yields to accumulate credits — need chargeback rules and per-tenant quotas.
- KV affinity hints: rely on customer-provided conversation_id vs hashing prompt tokens — both have failure modes. Conservative default should not require customer opt-in.
- Memory overhead: per-window metadata per-GPU must stay small; need a cap on active windows.

Implementation roadmap (rough):
- Week 0–1: prototype selector/evaluator + scoring library; unit tests for scoring heuristics.
- Week 2–3: implement window lifecycle + compaction on single-worker simulator; synthetic harness A/B.
- Week 4: KV-hit-rate sampler and credit-accounting prototype.
- Week 5–6: integrate with real serving-runtime worker loop behind feature-flag; telemetry hooks.
- Week 7–8: staging experiments + tuning.

Short pseudo-flow (simplified):
1) req -> admission: estimate size -> quick candidate lookup by kernel_signature bucket
2) compute top candidate score(s) (fast heuristics path uses cached top-N)
3) if score >= threshold: append request tokens into window (possibly split across windows if needed)
4) else create new small window and schedule
5) after window emit: if underfilled, donate tokens (earn credits) to queued short requests

Notes & TODOs:
- TODO: add a compact spec for the score function and a default set of weights to try in staging (start: kernel_match=0.6, kv_affinity=0.2, remaining_capacity=0.1, inactivity_penalty=0.1, priority_boost dynamic).
- TODO: small benchmark harness to measure kernel_switch latency impact (instrument time lost to kernel rebinding).
- TODO: design per-tenant throttles to avoid credit-economy exploits.
- TODO: doc a graceful rollback story for prod if compaction causes regressions.

Appendix: test-case examples (literal)
- Example 1: two concurrent requests: R1 long(1024 tokens, model A), R2 short(12 tokens, model A). With fluid-windowing: R2 injected into short-window coalesced with same kernel_sig -> finishes quickly; R1 continues in long window, but earns credits when R2 consumed donated tokens. With naive token-only batching we might preempt R1's kernel leading to longer wall-time due to kernel rebind.
- Example 2: model A (fp16 kernel) interleaved with model B (int8 kernel). Coordinator should prefer distinct windows to avoid repeating kernel switches; compaction should only merge same-kernel windows.

If you
- agree with the direction: I can push a minimal simulator and prioritized list of weights for initial sweep.
- disagree: please call out specific tradeoffs (e.g., prefer simpler request-level fairness) — this can help refine the design decisions.

Signature: Miguel Sanchez (eng-serving-runtime) — draft notes, not final spec.
